definition: Buying and selling (or short-selling and buying back) the exact same stock within the same single trading day.
Buying and selling stocks within the same day to profit from small price moves, closing every position before the market closes.
Holding a stock for weeks, months, or years — the opposite approach from day trading.
Happening within a single trading day, like a price move or a trade that opens and closes before the market closes.
A marketplace, like the New York Stock Exchange or Nasdaq, where stocks are actually bought and sold.
The short letter code, like AAPL for Apple, used to identify a specific stock on an exchange.
The trading session before the official market open, usually thinner and choppier than regular hours.
The trading session after the official market close, usually thinner and choppier than regular hours.
The block of time, like the regular 9:30am-4pm ET US stock market hours, during which trading actually happens.
An order that buys or sells a stock immediately at the best price currently available, with no price guarantee.
An order that only buys or sells a stock at a specific price or better, even if that means it never fills.
An order that sits inactive until the stock hits a chosen price, then automatically turns into a market order.
A stop order that, once triggered, becomes a limit order instead of a market order, guaranteeing price but not guaranteeing it fills.
The highest price a buyer is currently willing to pay for a stock right now.
The lowest price a seller is currently willing to accept for a stock right now.
The gap between the current bid price and the current ask price of a stock.
How easily a stock can be bought or sold quickly without moving its price much, because there are lots of buyers and sellers.
The difference between the price you expected a trade to fill at and the price it actually filled at.
A licensed firm or platform, like a brokerage app, that you place stock orders through.
A brokerage account that lets you borrow money from your broker to buy more stock than your own cash could afford.
A brokerage account where you can only trade with money you actually have deposited, with no borrowing allowed.
The total dollar amount of stock you're allowed to purchase right now, including any money your broker lets you borrow.
Using borrowed money to control a bigger stock position than your own cash alone could buy, which multiplies both gains and losses.
The software — a broker's own app or a separate program — you actually use to look at charts, place orders, and manage your account.
The part of a trading platform where you type or click to build and send a buy or sell order.
A saved list of stocks a trader keeps on their platform to track closely without holding a position in them yet.
Software focused mainly on displaying and analyzing price charts, sometimes separate from the platform you actually place orders on.
Live, up-to-the-second price and quote data, as opposed to data that's delayed by several minutes.
A data feed showing every current bid and ask price waiting in line for a stock, not just the single best bid and ask.
A single keyboard shortcut, set up in advance, that instantly sends a specific order — used on desktop platforms so a trade doesn't need several clicks to fire.
The fee a broker charges for executing a trade; most US stock brokers dropped this to zero for ordinary stock and ETF trades.
Money a broker earns by routing your order to a particular market maker to fill, which is part of how many brokers offer commission-free trading.
The Financial Industry Regulatory Authority, the US organization that writes and enforces the rulebook brokers must follow.
The Securities and Exchange Commission, the US government agency that regulates the stock markets and protects investors.

A historical FINRA label for a margin-account trader making 4+ day trades in 5 business days; it required $25,000 minimum equity until that requirement was eliminated in June 2026 in favor of new intraday margin rules.
The 2026 FINRA rule that replaced the old $25,000 pattern-day-trader minimum, requiring brokers to hold equity in proportion to how much a trader is actually exposed to during the trading day.
A single chart symbol showing a stock's open, close, high, and low price for one time period, shaped like a candle with a body and wicks.
The thin line above or below a candlestick's body, showing the highest and lowest prices reached during that period.
The thick rectangular part of a candlestick showing the distance between the opening price and the closing price.
A candlestick where the closing price ended higher than the opening price, usually colored green or white.
A candlestick where the closing price ended lower than the opening price, usually colored red or black.
The length of time each candlestick or bar on a chart represents, like 1 minute, 5 minutes, or 1 day.
Another name for the timeframe setting that controls how much time each single candlestick on a chart covers.
A price level where a falling stock has historically stopped dropping because enough buyers stepped in.
A price level where a rising stock has historically stopped climbing because enough sellers stepped in.
When a stock's price pushes through a resistance level and keeps climbing past it, instead of turning back down.
When a stock's price pushes through a support level and keeps falling past it, instead of bouncing back up.
A stretch of time where a stock's price is generally making higher highs and higher lows, moving upward overall.
A stretch of time where a stock's price is generally making lower highs and lower lows, moving downward overall.
A straight line drawn across a chart connecting a stock's recent highs or lows to show the direction it's been moving.
A stock moving sideways between a fairly steady support level and resistance level, without a clear up or down trend.
The number of shares of a stock that actually changed hands, bought and sold, during a given time period.
A sudden, much-larger-than-usual burst of shares trading hands, often signaling unusually strong interest in a stock.
A line that smooths out a stock's price by averaging it over a set number of recent periods, like the last 50 days.
Simple moving average: a moving average that weights every price in its lookback period equally, with no extra emphasis on recent prices.
Exponential moving average: a moving average that gives more weight to recent prices, so it reacts to new price moves faster than an SMA.
A signal traders watch for when a faster moving average crosses above or below a slower moving average, often read as a shift in trend.
Relative Strength Index: an indicator from 0 to 100 that measures how fast and how far a stock's price has recently moved, used to spot overbought or oversold conditions.
A stock whose price has risen so far, so fast that it's considered due for a pullback, often flagged by a high RSI reading.
A stock whose price has fallen so far, so fast that it's considered due for a bounce, often flagged by a low RSI reading.
Moving Average Convergence Divergence: an indicator that compares two moving averages to show shifts in a stock's momentum and trend direction.
A chart pattern where a stock rallies to about the same high price twice, with a dip in between, often signaling a reversal downward.
A chart pattern where a stock falls to about the same low price twice, with a bounce in between, often signaling a reversal upward.
A chart pattern with three peaks — a higher middle peak flanked by two lower ones — often signaling an uptrend is about to reverse.
A chart pattern where price pauses and drifts sideways or slightly against the trend in a small rectangle shape, before continuing the original trend.
The number of shares (or the dollar amount) you buy in a single trade, chosen to match how much risk you're willing to take.
The total current dollar value of everything in your trading account, cash plus the market value of any open positions.
The dollar amount, usually a small percent of account equity, you're willing to lose on a single trade if it goes wrong.
A pre-set order that automatically sells a stock once it drops to a chosen price, capping how much you can lose on that trade.
A pre-set order that automatically sells a stock once it rises to a chosen price, locking in a planned gain.
How much you stand to lose on a trade compared to how much you stand to gain if it works out, like risking $1 to make $3.
A fixed dollar amount that, once lost in a single day, means you stop trading for the rest of that day no matter what.
The drop from an account's highest recent value down to a lower point, measured in dollars or as a percentage.
A demand from your broker to deposit more money immediately, because losses on borrowed (margin) trades have eaten into your required equity.
Borrowing or sizing a position so large relative to your account that even a small adverse price move can wipe out a large share of your equity.
Fear of missing out: the anxious urge to jump into a trade late, just because a stock is moving fast and you don't want to miss the gain.
Immediately making a new, often oversized trade to try to win back money just lost, instead of following your normal plan.
A state of emotional frustration after a loss that pushes a trader into impulsive, undisciplined decisions.
Placing far more trades than your plan calls for, often driven by boredom, excitement, or trying to force profits.
A written log where a trader records every trade's setup, reasoning, result, and lessons learned to review later.
Testing a set of trading rules against past price data to see how it would have performed before ever risking real money on it.
The percentage of a trader's total trades that ended as winners, out of every trade taken.
A trader's own written rulebook covering what to trade, when to enter and exit, how much to risk, and how to review results.
A specific, written condition in a trading plan that must be true before opening a new trade.
A specific, written condition in a trading plan that decides when to close a trade, whether it's winning or losing.
The overall method a trader uses to find trades, such as trading breakouts or trading pullbacks to a moving average.
Practicing trades with fake, simulated money on a real price feed so mistakes don't cost anything while still learning.
A brokerage account funded with simulated money instead of real cash, used to paper trade a strategy risk-free.
The ticker symbol for Apple stock on the exchange.
The New York Stock Exchange, one of the largest stock exchanges in the world.
